terms.grammar: phrase: inter with the reflexive, or with nōs, vōs
evidence: Cic. Att. 6.1.12: Cicerōnēs puerī amant inter sē
Cic. Att. 14.13B.5: ut nōsmet ipsī inter nōs conjūnctiōrēs sīmus (Lewis & Short, s.v. conjungō)
terms.comment: The classical way, with any verb: amant inter sē, they love each other; inter nōs for us, inter vōs for you.

terms.grammar: phrase: alter twice, the second in the case the verb needs
evidence: Sen. Ep. 7.11: alter alterī theātrum sumus
terms.comment: alter alterī theātrum sumus, we are an audience for each other. Of more than two, alius alium.
In this sense from Livy on, mostly post-Augustan (Pliny, Tacitus, Quintilian), not in Cicero; classically it means “in turn” (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Cicerōnēs puerī amant inter sē, exercentur, sed discunt, alter … frēnīs eget, alter calcāribus
phrases.english: The boys Cicero love each other, they play together, but they learn too; one … needs the reins, the other the spurs.

phrases.latin: vetus verbum hoc quidem est: commūnia esse amīcōrum inter sē omnia
phrases.english: It’s an old saying, at any rate, that friends have everything in common with each other.

phrases.latin: satis enim magnum alter alterī theātrum sumus
phrases.english: For we are a big enough audience for each other.

phrases.latin: paulisper alter alterīus cōnspectū, admīrātiōne mūtuā prope attonitī, conticuēre
phrases.english: For a little while, each at the sight of the other, almost stunned with mutual admiration, they fell silent.

phrases.latin: cūnctātī aliquamdiū sunt, dum alius alium, ut proelium incipiant, circumspectant
phrases.english: They hung back for some time, while each looked round at the others to start the fight.

phrases.latin: sunt etiam nōnnūllī acuendīs puerōrum ingeniīs nōn inūtilēs lūsūs, cum positīs invicem cujusque generis quaestiunculīs aemulantur
phrases.english: There are also some games, not useless for sharpening children’s wits, when they compete by setting each other little questions of every kind.

phrases.latin: frīgoribus partō agricolae plērumque fruuntur mūtuaque inter sē laetī convīvia cūrant. invītat geniālis hiems cūrāsque resolvit
phrases.english: In the cold the farmers mostly enjoy what they have earned, and, happy, give dinners for each other in turn; festive winter invites them and loosens their cares.
